chapter: Meeting Jay McShann and Martin's on the Plaza
title: McShann as pianist and the band's ballad repertoire
summary: McShann was loved as a pianist; at Martin's they played pop tunes more than hot ones.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Well, it was personality, but he was really playing the piano. He came in --
Well, I know, but I wonder whether they really appreciated how much piano work -- appreciate these piano players?

Oh, yeah, they did. They had him on some afternoons, he'd have to go down to that music store. I think it's Deacon's Music. If I'm not getting them mixed up with the music stores in Texas, now. But that big music store down there on -- was it Baltimore? Anyway, right down in the heart of town, Thamon Hayes was working as a salesman.
Well, that was after Thamon Hayes --
After his band broke up. He'd go down there in the afternoons, different people, professors from the college and teaching, and everything, they'd go
go down and have him come down and play for them, you know. they loved it far Everbody was crazy about his playing, a lot more than anybody in Kansas City.

How much more -- you know, when we first saw -- knew of him, we figure he's like a blues and boogie-woogie pianist. Now, when he came to record for Weibacker five or six years ago, that was the first time I realized that he could play ballads so beautifully.

Let me say this: People think of him and of Bird as guys who were playing bluesy and all jazz, you know. But McShann's band, when we worked out that morning on the Plaza, we played things like "Hawaiian Paradise," and "Somewhere Over the Rainbow," "Sierra Sue". This is mostly what we played. We only played those, what you'd say hot tunes -- certain times.
